result:
The town hired a man to remove its clocks.

No one could remember voting for this, but the paperwork was impeccable, and he arrived on a Tuesday with a ladder, a toolbox, and a sandwich wrapped in wax paper.

He started at the railway station.

“What about the trains?” asked the stationmaster.

“They’ll still arrive,” said the man.

“When?”

“That’s mostly their business already.”

By Thursday, the clock above the pharmacy was gone. On Friday, he took down the school clocks. The children discovered that the last ten minutes before lunch could survive perfectly well without a face or hands.

People kept checking their wrists, even those who had never worn watches.

At the bakery, a woman asked when the bread would be ready.

“When the crust is right,” said the baker, and found he liked saying it.

There were difficulties. Two lovers missed each other by an afternoon. A council meeting continued until someone opened the curtains and discovered it was dark. The church bell rang whenever Mr. Bellamy remembered, which gave Sundays an uncertain, generous shape.

The last clock stood in the square.

The man climbed his ladder while a small crowd watched. Inside the clock’s casing, behind the gears, he found a bird’s nest, empty except for a blue thread and a receipt from a shop that had closed twenty years before.

He brought the nest down carefully.

“Is that what was wrong with it?” a girl asked.

“Nothing was wrong with it.”

“Then why take it away?”

He looked toward the municipal offices. Nobody came out.

For the first time all week, he unfolded the paperwork.

The crowd waited while he read it.

“Oh,” he said.

The town had hired him to remove its *moss*.

Someone fetched the stationmaster. Someone else went home for a bucket. The man sat on the edge of the fountain and ate his sandwich.

By dusk, three clocks were back in place.

The baker asked whether they might leave his until Monday.
